techniques.name: Statistical Oversampling Methods
techniques.description: Statistical oversampling methods rebalance a training set by adding synthetic examples of an under-represented category instead of copying existing ones. The foundational method, SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), takes a minority-class example, picks one of its nearest minority-class neighbours, and creates a new example at a random point on the line between the two in feature space. Variants differ in which examples seed the new points, such as Borderline-SMOTE (examples near the class boundary), ADASYN (examples with many neighbours from the other class) and SVMSMOTE (the support vectors of a support vector machine). Standard SMOTE balances the outcome labels and ignores group membership, so for fairness work the same generation is applied within each combination of protected group and label, making every combination equally large in the training data. Only the training data change, and plain SMOTE needs numeric features, with SMOTE-NC covering a mix of numeric and categorical ones.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's credit team finds that approved applicants from one ethnic group make up a small share of its loan training data. It adds synthetic approved applicants for that group with SMOTE until every group-and-outcome combination is the same size, then compares the approval-rate gap between groups, and the gap in approval of applicants who went on to repay, on held-out applications against a model trained on the original data.

A hospital analytics team building a readmission model finds that patients from one small ethnic group rarely appear among the readmitted cases. It applies Borderline-SMOTE within each group's readmitted cases, then reports recall for each group on held-out patients, with and without oversampling, to its clinical safety committee before deployment.

A university's student-support team builds a dropout-risk model from past cohorts in which students from low-income areas who left are few. It uses ADASYN to add synthetic examples for that combination, then checks on held-out cohorts that the model flags those students at a rate no further below the rate for other students than the model trained on the original data.

limitations.description: Plain SMOTE and its variants balance the outcome labels, not the groups, and can widen group gaps. In one study (logistic regression on the Adult income data), SMOTE raised the statistical parity difference between sexes from 0.21 to 0.33 (Chakraborty et al., 2021). Balancing protected-group-and-label combinations is needed for fairness, and the gaps must be measured on held-out data.

Synthetic points are interpolated from the few real examples already present, so they add no new information about a small group and do not repair why it is under-represented, such as how the data were collected. Counts on the oversampled set look larger than the real evidence behind them.

Interpolation assumes the space between two minority examples also belongs to the minority class. Where examples are scattered, overlap the majority class or include outliers, new points land in the wrong region and add label noise. ADASYN, which favours hard cases, can concentrate on outliers.

In high-dimensional data SMOTE mostly fails to correct the lean towards the majority class and is less effective than random undersampling. It lowers variability and makes synthetic points correlated, and with k-nearest-neighbour classifiers and no feature selection it tips predictions towards the minority class (Blagus and Lusa, 2013).

Oversampling before splitting the data, or before cross-validation, leaks information into the test set and inflates results. Resampling must touch only the training part, for example inside an imbalanced-learn Pipeline, and tests should use the natural class mix.

resources.title: SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique
resources.abstract: An approach to the construction of classifiers from    imbalanced datasets is described. A dataset is imbalanced if the    classification categories are not approximately equally    represented. Often real-world data sets are predominately composed of    ``normal'' examples with only a small percentage of ``abnormal'' or    ``interesting'' examples. It is also the case that the cost of    misclassifying an abnormal (interesting) example as a normal example    is often much higher than the cost of the reverse    error. Under-sampling of the majority (normal) class has been proposed    as a good means of increasing the sensitivity of a classifier to the    minority class. This paper shows that a combination of our method of    over-sampling the minority (abnormal) class and under-sampling the    majority (normal) class can achieve better classifier performance (in    ROC space) than only under-sampling the majority class.  This paper    also shows that a combination of our method of over-sampling the    minority class and under-sampling the majority class can achieve    better classifier performance (in ROC space) than varying the loss    ratios in Ripper or class priors in Naive Bayes. Our method of    over-sampling the minority class involves creating synthetic minority    class examples.  Experiments are performed using C4.5, Ripper and a    Naive Bayes classifier. The method is evaluated using the area under    the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC) and the ROC convex    hull strategy.

resources.title: ADASYN: Adaptive synthetic sampling approach for imbalanced learning
resources.abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive synthetic (ADASYN) sampling approach for learning from imbalanced data sets. The essential idea of ADASYN is to use a weighted distribution for different minority class examples according to their level of difficulty in learning, where more synthetic data is generated for minority class examples that are harder to learn compared to those minority examples that are easier to learn. As a result, the ADASYN approach improves learning with respect to the data distributions in two ways: (1) reducing the bias introduced by the class imbalance, and (2) adaptively shifting the classification decision boundary toward the difficult examples. Simulation analyses on several machine learning data sets show the effectiveness of this method across five evaluation metrics.

resources.title: SMOTE for high-dimensional class-imbalanced data
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Classification using class-imbalanced data is biased in favor of the majority class. The bias is even larger for high-dimensional data, where the number of variables greatly exceeds the number of samples. The problem can be attenuated by undersampling or oversampling, which produce class-balanced data. Generally undersampling is helpful, while random oversampling is not. Synthetic Minority Oversampling TEchnique (SMOTE) is a very popular oversampling method that was proposed to improve random oversampling but its behavior on high-dimensional data has not been thoroughly investigated. In this paper we investigate the properties of SMOTE from a theoretical and empirical point of view, using simulated and real high-dimensional data. RESULTS: While in most cases SMOTE seems beneficial with low-dimensional data, it does not attenuate the bias towards the classification in the majority class for most classifiers when data are high-dimensional, and it is less effective than random undersampling. SMOTE is beneficial for k-NN classifiers for high-dimensional data if the number of variables is reduced performing some type of variable selection; we explain why, otherwise, the k-NN classification is biased towards the minority class. Furthermore, we show that on high-dimensional data SMOTE does not change the class-specific mean values while it decreases the data variability and it introduces correlation between samples. We explain how our findings impact the class-prediction for high-dimensional data. CONCLUSIONS: In practice, in the high-dimensional setting only k-NN classifiers based on the Euclidean distance seem to benefit substantially from the use of SMOTE, provided that variable selection is performed before using SMOTE; the benefit is larger if more neighbors are used. SMOTE for k-NN without variable selection should not be used, because it strongly biases the classification towards the minority class.

resources.title: A Comparison of Undersampling, Oversampling, and SMOTE Methods for Dealing with Imbalanced Classification in Educational Data Mining
resources.abstract: Educational data mining is capable of producing useful data-driven applications (e.g., early warning systems in schools or the prediction of students’ academic achievement) based on predictive models. However, the class imbalance problem in educational datasets could hamper the accuracy of predictive models as many of these models are designed on the assumption that the predicted class is balanced. Although previous studies proposed several methods to deal with the imbalanced class problem, most of them focused on the technical details of how to improve each technique, while only a few focused on the application aspect, especially for the application of data with different imbalance ratios. In this study, we compared several sampling techniques to handle the different ratios of the class imbalance problem (i.e., moderately or extremely imbalanced classifications) using the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009 dataset. For our comparison, we used random oversampling (ROS), random undersampling (RUS), and the combination of the synthetic minority oversampling technique for nominal and continuous (SMOTE-NC) and RUS as a hybrid resampling technique. We used the Random Forest as our classification algorithm to evaluate the results of each sampling technique. Our results show that random oversampling for moderately imbalanced data and hybrid resampling for extremely imbalanced data seem to work best. The implications for educational data mining applications and suggestions for future research are discussed.

sample_claims.text: The credit model was trained on data in which approved and refused applicants from each ethnic group were equally represented, using synthetic examples generated within each group-and-outcome combination, and its approval-rate gap between groups on held-out applicants is reported against the same model trained on the original data.

Oversampling by ethnic group and outcome did not widen the gap in recall between groups for the readmission model: recall for each group on held-out patients is reported with and without oversampling.
The dropout-risk model flags students from low-income areas at a rate no further below that of other students than the same model trained without oversampling, measured on held-out cohorts.
Every combination of protected group and outcome has the same number of training examples, because synthetic examples were generated for each smaller combination up to the size of the largest.

techniques.name: Reweighing
techniques.description: Reweighing is a fairness method, presented by Kamiran and Calders (2012), that adjusts the training data before any model is trained so that a protected attribute, such as sex or ethnicity, has no statistical link to the outcome label. It does this by giving each training example a weight, leaving every feature value and label unchanged. Each combination of group and label (for example, women who were hired) gets a weight equal to the number of examples it would hold if group and label were unrelated, divided by the number it actually holds. Combinations rarer than that expectation, such as positive outcomes in a disadvantaged group, are weighted up and over-represented ones are weighted down, so every group has the same rate of positive labels in the weighted data. A model is then trained on the original data with these weights, so the learning algorithm must accept example weights.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model team finds that in the historical loan decisions used as training labels, applicants from one ethnic group were approved far less often than others. Before retraining its approval model it computes reweighing weights, so that approved applicants from that group count for more and refused ones for less, trains with them as sample weights, and compares the approval-rate gap and accuracy on held-out data against the unweighted model.

A health insurer's analytics team building a model to target postpartum depression outreach from Medicaid claims compares reweighing by race with simply removing race from the inputs. It reports each option's disparate impact ratio (the ratio of positive-prediction rates between groups) and predictive performance to its clinical governance group before choosing one.

A recruitment platform training a shortlisting model on past hiring outcomes, in which women were hired into senior engineering roles less often than men, applies reweighing by sex before training so that the weighted history shows equal hiring rates, then checks shortlisting rates by sex on a held-out set of applications.

limitations.description: Its target is fixed: equal rates of positive labels across groups in the weighted training data (statistical parity). It does not aim at equal error rates such as equal opportunity, and the weights are computed once, before training, so they cannot respond to where the trained model actually errs. An adaptive variant (Krasanakis et al., 2018) re-estimates weights during training for error-rate criteria, but it has no maintained implementation.

It removes all association between group and label, including any part a legitimate factor explains. Kamiran and Calders give the example of car insurance, where more accidents among men may justify different outcomes by sex; reweighing erases that difference too, so it over-corrects wherever some gap between groups is warranted.

The learning algorithm must accept example weights; where it cannot, the data have to be resampled instead, which is a different method. Only the training data are balanced, so the trained model's predictions are not guaranteed to be: outcome rates by group must be measured on held-out data after training rather than assumed.

When a group-label combination is rare its weight is large (a combination with a tenth of its expected count gets a weight of ten), so a handful of examples can dominate training. This raises variance and amplifies any labelling errors in exactly the group the method is meant to protect, and it bites hardest with small or intersectional groups.
An absent group-label combination cannot be created by weighting existing records. Zero observed counts require explicit handling rather than applying the ratio unchanged.

resources.title: Data preprocessing techniques for classification without discrimination
resources.abstract: Recently, the following Discrimination-Aware Classification Problem was introduced: Suppose we are given training data that exhibit unlawful discrimination; e.g., toward sensitive attributes such as gender or ethnicity. The task is to learn a classifier that optimizes accuracy, but does not have this discrimination in its predictions on test data. This problem is relevant in many settings, such as when the data are generated by a biased decision process or when the sensitive attribute serves as a proxy for unobserved features. In this paper, we concentrate on the case with only one binary sensitive attribute and a two-class classification problem. We first study the theoretically optimal trade-off between accuracy and non-discrimination for pure classifiers. Then, we look at algorithmic solutions that preprocess the data to remove discrimination before a classifier is learned. We survey and extend our existing data preprocessing techniques, being suppression of the sensitive attribute, massaging the dataset by changing class labels, and reweighing or resampling the data to remove discrimination without relabeling instances. These preprocessing techniques have been implemented in a modified version of Weka and we present the results of experiments on real-life data.

resources.title: Comparison of Methods to Reduce Bias From Clinical Prediction Models of Postpartum Depression
resources.abstract: Importance: The lack of standards in methods to reduce bias for clinical algorithms presents various challenges in providing reliable predictions and in addressing health disparities. Objective: To evaluate approaches for reducing bias in machine learning models using a real-world clinical scenario. Design, Setting, and Participants: Health data for this cohort study were obtained from the IBM MarketScan Medicaid Database. Eligibility criteria were as follows: (1) Female individuals aged 12 to 55 years with a live birth record identified by delivery-related codes from January 1, 2014, through December 31, 2018; (2) greater than 80% enrollment through pregnancy to 60 days post partum; and (3) evidence of coverage for depression screening and mental health services. Statistical analysis was performed in 2020. Exposures: Binarized race (Black individuals and White individuals). Main Outcomes and Measures: Machine learning models (logistic regression [LR], random forest, and extreme gradient boosting) were trained for 2 binary outcomes: postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum mental health service utilization. Risk-adjusted generalized linear models were used for each outcome to assess potential disparity in the cohort associated with binarized race (Black or White). Methods for reducing bias, including reweighing, Prejudice Remover, and removing race from the models, were examined by analyzing changes in fairness metrics compared with the base models. Baseline characteristics of female individuals at the top-predicted risk decile were compared for systematic differences. Fairness metrics of disparate impact (DI, 1 indicates fairness) and equal opportunity difference (EOD, 0 indicates fairness). Results: Among 573 634 female individuals initially examined for this study, 314 903 were White (54.9%), 217 899 were Black (38.0%), and the mean (SD) age was 26.1 (5.5) years. The risk-adjusted odds ratio comparing White participants with Black participants was 2.06 (95% CI, 2.02-2.10) for clinically recognized PPD and 1.37 (95% CI, 1.33-1.40) for postpartum mental health service utilization. Taking the LR model for PPD prediction as an example, reweighing reduced bias as measured by improved DI and EOD metrics from 0.31 and -0.19 to 0.79 and 0.02, respectively. Removing race from the models had inferior performance for reducing bias compared with the other methods (PPD: DI = 0.61; EOD = -0.05; mental health service utilization: DI = 0.63; EOD = -0.04). Conclusions and Relevance: Clinical prediction models trained on potentially biased data may produce unfair outcomes on the basis of the chosen metrics. This study's results suggest that the performance varied depending on the model, outcome label, and method for reducing bias. This approach toward evaluating algorithmic bias can be used as an example for the growing number of researchers who wish to examine and address bias in their data and models.

resources.title: Bias Discovery in Machine Learning Models for Mental Health
resources.abstract: Fairness and bias are crucial concepts in artificial intelligence, yet they are relatively ignored in machine learning applications in clinical psychiatry. We computed fairness metrics and present bias mitigation strategies using a model trained on clinical mental health data. We collected structured data related to the admission, diagnosis, and treatment of patients in the psychiatry department of the University Medical Center Utrecht. We trained a machine learning model to predict future administrations of benzodiazepines on the basis of past data. We found that gender plays an unexpected role in the predictions—this constitutes bias. Using the AI Fairness 360 package, we implemented reweighing and discrimination-aware regularization as bias mitigation strategies, and we explored their implications for model performance. This is the first application of bias exploration and mitigation in a machine learning model trained on real clinical psychiatry data.

sample_claims.text: The approval model was trained on loan history reweighed so that every ethnic group has the same approval rate in the weighted data, and its approval-rate gap on held-out applicants is reported alongside its accuracy.
The postpartum depression outreach model, trained with reweighing by race, has a disparate impact ratio within the agreed range on held-out patients.
The shortlisting model's training data were reweighed by sex before training, and shortlisting rates by sex on held-out applications fall within the agreed tolerance.

techniques.name: Disparate Impact Remover
techniques.description: Disparate Impact Remover is a pre-processing method that edits the numerical features of a dataset so that they reveal less about a protected attribute such as race or sex. For each feature it compares how the values are distributed within each protected group, then moves every value towards a shared distribution while keeping its rank within its own group, so people near the top of their group stay near the top. The user sets a repair level from 0 (no change) to 1 (each feature is distributed identically in every group). The aim is to avoid disparate impact, where one group's selection rate falls below 80 per cent of the most favoured group's rate. Stronger repair narrows that gap but costs predictive accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's data science team finds that income, length of employment and credit history length in its loan dataset differ systematically between applicants under and over 25. It repairs those three features at a level of 0.8, trains its scoring model on the repaired data, and checks the approval-rate ratio between the age groups against the 80 per cent threshold to decide whether a stronger repair is needed.

A fire service reviewing a promotion process finds that written and oral exam scores differ between ethnic groups, so a 70 per cent pass mark selects far fewer candidates from one group. It repairs both scores while keeping each candidate's rank within their own group, then checks whether the repaired scores still separate stronger candidates from weaker ones.

limitations.description: Repair costs predictive accuracy, and the cost varies sharply by dataset. In the original experiments a full repair cut a measure of classifier utility on the German credit data from about 72 per cent to about 50 per cent, close to chance, but the Adult income data lost only about two points. The repair level has to be chosen and justified.

It repairs numerical features only, and the AIF360 implementation takes one protected attribute at a time. Categorical features such as job title or postcode are left unchanged and can still carry the protected attribute, and repairing several attributes together means the user must define the joint groups.

Each feature is repaired separately, so every feature can look identical across groups while combinations of features still reveal the protected attribute. A model trained on several repaired features may therefore still show disparate impact, which is why the original paper pairs the repair with a test that tries to predict the protected attribute from all the features together.

The repair depends on each person's protected attribute and on the group distributions seen in the training data. AIF360 notes that new data can be transformed the same way only if those conditional distributions match, and each new record needs its protected attribute, which makes the method awkward for a live scoring service.

The target is the US 80 per cent rule, a comparison of group selection rates, and the paper notes that other legal frameworks may need a different formulation. The rule says nothing about how individuals are treated, and the paper points out that disparate impact is not itself unlawful where a business necessity can be shown.

resources.title: Certifying and Removing Disparate Impact
resources.abstract: What does it mean for an algorithm to be biased? In U.S. law, unintentional bias is encoded via disparate impact, which occurs when a selection process has widely different outcomes for different groups, even as it appears to be neutral. This legal determination hinges on a definition of a protected class (ethnicity, gender) and an explicit description of the process. When computers are involved, determining disparate impact (and hence bias) is harder. It might not be possible to disclose the process. In addition, even if the process is open, it might be hard to elucidate in a legal setting how the algorithm makes its decisions. Instead of requiring access to the process, we propose making inferences based on the data it uses. We present four contributions. First, we link disparate impact to a measure of classification accuracy that while known, has received relatively little attention. Second, we propose a test for disparate impact based on how well the protected class can be predicted from the other attributes. Third, we describe methods by which data might be made unbiased. Finally, we present empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of our test for disparate impact and our approach for both masking bias and preserving relevant information in the data. Interestingly, our approach resembles some actual selection practices that have recently received legal scrutiny.

resources.title: A comparative study of fairness-enhancing interventions in machine learning
resources.abstract: Computers are increasingly used to make decisions that have significant impact on people's lives. Often, these predictions can affect different population subgroups disproportionately. As a result, the issue of fairness has received much recent interest, and a number of fairness-enhanced classifiers have appeared in the literature. This paper seeks to study the following questions: how do these different techniques fundamentally compare to one another, and what accounts for the differences? Specifically, we seek to bring attention to many under-appreciated aspects of such fairness-enhancing interventions that require investigation for these algorithms to receive broad adoption.

resources.title: Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

sample_claims.text: After repair at level 1.0, the income, employment length and credit history features in the lending dataset have the same distribution for applicants under and over 25.
A classifier trained to predict applicants' age group from the repaired features performs no better than chance.
Repairing the promotion exam scores kept each candidate's rank within their ethnic group and raised the ratio of group pass rates above the 80 per cent threshold.
The loss in predictive accuracy caused by the repair is documented and stays within the tolerance agreed with the credit risk team.

techniques.name: Fairness GAN
techniques.description: Fairness GAN is a pre-processing method that generates a synthetic training dataset in which decisions no longer track a protected attribute such as gender or skin tone. A generative adversarial network (GAN) is a pair of networks trained against each other, one producing fake examples and one trying to tell them from real ones. Here the generator is conditioned on the protected attribute and produces both an example and its decision label, such as hired or rejected (images in the original work, table rows in Xu et al.'s separate FairGAN). An extra network tries to predict the protected attribute from the generated output, and the generator is rewarded for defeating it, so favourable decisions become more similar across groups. The user can aim for demographic parity, meaning equal rates of favourable decisions, or for equality of opportunity, which applies the constraint only to favourable decisions.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment technology team holds interview-video stills labelled with past shortlisting decisions that favoured one gender. It trains a Fairness GAN to generate a synthetic image set whose shortlisting labels are similar for women and men, trains the screening model on that set, and compares shortlisting rates by gender on held-out real images before deployment.

A lender's data science team has ten years of loan decisions in which women were approved less often than men on similar incomes. It trains a tabular FairGAN-style generator to produce a synthetic dataset, confirms that the gap in approval rates in the synthetic data is close to zero, and trains its scoring model on that data, testing accuracy and approval rates on real held-out applications.

limitations.description: GAN training is unstable and the fairness loss adds a further pull on the generator. The original authors used spectral normalisation, softened outcome values and added noise to keep training stable, and results still varied across datasets. Expect tuning effort and repeated runs.

Fairness and accuracy trade off, and the gain is uneven. In the original experiments a classifier trained on debiased CelebA data went from about 20 to about 29 per cent error. Demographic parity improved on three of four datasets but not on Quick, Draw!, and the demographic-parity version made equality of opportunity worse on the soccer data.

It needs a lot of data. The authors had only 1,501 labelled soccer images, so they borrowed more than 200,000 unlabelled CelebA faces to help the generator, which is possible only when a large related set exists.

The original method covers a narrow setting: image inputs, one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome, with demographic parity or equality of opportunity but not equalised odds. Continuous protected attributes and non-image data are left as future work, and tabular versions such as FairGAN are separate methods with their own evidence.

Fairness is judged by training a classifier on the synthetic data and testing it on real data, and image quality is judged mainly by inspecting average faces. The authors report that debiasing visibly changes images in stereotyped ways, such as male faces taking on features coded as feminine, so the synthetic data need checking for distortions that the classifier test would miss.

resources.title: Fairness GAN
resources.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Fairness GAN, an approach for generating a dataset that is plausibly similar to a given multimedia dataset, but is more fair with respect to protected attributes in allocative decision making. We propose a novel auxiliary classifier GAN that strives for demographic parity or equality of opportunity and show empirical results on several datasets, including the CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA) dataset, the Quick, Draw!\ dataset, and a dataset of soccer player images and the offenses they were called for. The proposed formulation is well-suited to absorbing unlabeled data; we leverage this to augment the soccer dataset with the much larger CelebA dataset. The methodology tends to improve demographic parity and equality of opportunity while generating plausible images.

resources.title: FairGAN: Fairness-aware Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Fairness-aware learning is increasingly important in data mining. Discrimination prevention aims to prevent discrimination in the training data before it is used to conduct predictive analysis. In this paper, we focus on fair data generation that ensures the generated data is discrimination free. Inspired by generative adversarial networks (GAN), we present fairness-aware generative adversarial networks, called FairGAN, which are able to learn a generator producing fair data and also preserving good data utility. Compared with the naive fair data generation models, FairGAN further ensures the classifiers which are trained on generated data can achieve fair classification on real data. Experiments on a real dataset show the effectiveness of FairGAN.

resources.title: Bt-GAN: Generating Fair Synthetic Healthdata via Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Synthetic data generation offers a promising solution to enhance the usefulness of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) by generating realistic de-identified data. However, the existing literature primarily focuses on the quality of synthetic health data, neglecting the crucial aspect of fairness in downstream predictions. Consequently, models trained on synthetic EHR have faced criticism for producing biased outcomes in target tasks. These biases can arise from either spurious correlations between features or the failure of models to accurately represent sub-groups. To address these concerns, we present Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks (Bt-GAN), a GAN-based synthetic data generator specifically designed for the healthcare domain. In order to tackle spurious correlations (i), we propose an information-constrained Data Generation Process (DGP) that enables the generator to learn a fair deterministic transformation based on a well-defined notion of algorithmic fairness. To overcome the challenge of capturing exact sub-group representations (ii), we incentivize the generator to preserve sub-group densities through score-based weighted sampling. This approach compels the generator to learn from underrepresented regions of the data manifold. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Our results demonstrate that Bt-GAN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while significantly improving fairness and minimizing bias amplification. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth explainability analysis to provide additional evidence supporting the validity of our study. In conclusion, our research introduces a novel and professional approach to addressing the limitations of synthetic data generation in the healthcare domain. By incorporating fairness considerations and leveraging advanced techniques such as GANs, we pave the way for more reliable and unbiased predictions in healthcare applications.

resources.title: FairFinGAN: Fairness-Aware Synthetic Financial Data Generation
resources.abstract: Financial datasets often suffer from bias that can lead to unfair decision-making in automated systems. In this work, we propose FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based framework designed to generate synthetic financial data while mitigating bias with respect to the protected attribute. Our approach incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process through a classifier, ensuring that the synthetic data is both fair and preserves utility for downstream predictive tasks. We evaluate our proposed model on five real-world financial datasets and compare it with existing GAN-based data generation methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior fairness metrics without significant loss in data utility, demonstrating its potential as a tool for bias-aware data generation in financial applications.

sample_claims.text: In the synthetic training set generated for the screening model, the rate of favourable shortlisting decisions for women and men differs by less than the tolerance set in the project's fairness requirement.
A credit scoring model trained on the synthetic loan data shows a smaller gap in approval rates between women and men, on held-out real applications, than a model trained on the original data.
The synthetic data remain close enough to the original for the model's purpose: the accuracy cost of training on them, compared with the original data, was measured and judged acceptable.

techniques.name: Relabelling
techniques.description: Relabelling, also called data massaging, is a pre-processing method proposed by Kamiran and Calders. It changes some of the outcome labels in a training set so that a protected group and everyone else have the same rate of positive outcomes, such as being hired or approved. A ranking model first scores each example by how likely it is to be positive. The method then promotes the highest-scoring negative examples from the disadvantaged group to positive and demotes the lowest-scoring positive examples from the favoured group to negative, in equal numbers. Because the examples closest to the decision boundary change first and the numbers are equal, the overall share of positive labels stays the same and the number of changes is as small as it can be.

example_use_cases.description: A public-sector recruiter's ten years of shortlisting records show women shortlisted less often than men with comparable applications. Before training a screening model, the data team flips the labels of the rejected women a ranking model scores highest and the shortlisted men it scores lowest, in equal numbers, until shortlisting rates match and the overall shortlisting rate is unchanged.

A building society finds that past loan decisions approved applicants from one ethnic minority far less often than others with similar finances, and suspects the gap reflects past discretion rather than risk. It flips borderline decisions in both directions, keeping the overall approval rate fixed, and trains its scoring model on the corrected labels while keeping the original labels in a separate file.

limitations.description: It assumes the whole gap in positive rates between groups is discrimination. The number of labels changed is set to bring the gap to zero, even where part of the gap has a legitimate explanation, and the original authors note that such constraints are often too strong.

It rewrites the record of what happened. The flipped labels no longer match the real decisions or outcomes, so it suits labels that record biased past decisions and is dangerous where labels are measured facts, such as a confirmed diagnosis or a repayment. The authors call the approach intrusive.

Which records are flipped depends on a ranking model trained on the same biased data. A poor ranker flips the wrong people, and in the original experiments the discrimination and accuracy of the final classifier varied with the learner trained afterwards.

It handles one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome. Gender and ethnicity together, or a numeric attribute such as income, are not covered, so correcting one attribute can leave intersectional gaps.

Accuracy falls as discrimination falls, and the authors prove the trade-off cannot be avoided. Discrimination is removed from the training data, but a model trained on it can still show some on new data.

resources.title: Data preprocessing techniques for classification without discrimination
resources.abstract: Recently, the following Discrimination-Aware Classification Problem was introduced: Suppose we are given training data that exhibit unlawful discrimination; e.g., toward sensitive attributes such as gender or ethnicity. The task is to learn a classifier that optimizes accuracy, but does not have this discrimination in its predictions on test data. This problem is relevant in many settings, such as when the data are generated by a biased decision process or when the sensitive attribute serves as a proxy for unobserved features. In this paper, we concentrate on the case with only one binary sensitive attribute and a two-class classification problem. We first study the theoretically optimal trade-off between accuracy and non-discrimination for pure classifiers. Then, we look at algorithmic solutions that preprocess the data to remove discrimination before a classifier is learned. We survey and extend our existing data preprocessing techniques, being suppression of the sensitive attribute, massaging the dataset by changing class labels, and reweighing or resampling the data to remove discrimination without relabeling instances. These preprocessing techniques have been implemented in a modified version of Weka and we present the results of experiments on real-life data.

resources.title: Classifying without discriminating
resources.abstract: Classification models usually make predictions on the basis of training data. If the training data is biased towards certain groups or classes of objects, e.g., there is racial discrimination towards black people, the learned model will also show discriminatory behavior towards that particular community. This partial attitude of the learned model may lead to biased outcomes when labeling future unlabeled data objects. Often, however, impartial classification results are desired or even required by law for future data objects in spite of having biased training data. In this paper, we tackle this problem by introducing a new classification scheme for learning unbiased models on biased training data. Our method is based on massaging the dataset by making the least intrusive modifications which lead to an unbiased dataset. On this modified dataset we then learn a non-discriminating classifier. The proposed method has been implemented and experimental results on a credit approval dataset show promising results: in all experiments our method is able to reduce the prejudicial behavior for future classification significantly without loosing too much predictive accuracy.

sample_claims.text: In the corrected training set the share of positive labels is the same for women and men, and the overall share of positive labels is unchanged from the original data.
Only borderline cases, the examples nearest the ranking model's decision boundary, had their labels changed, in equal numbers in each direction, and no feature values were altered.
The lending model trained on the corrected labels shows a smaller gap in approval rates between age groups on held-out data than a model trained on the original labels.

techniques.name: Preferential Sampling
techniques.description: Preferential Sampling is a pre-processing method, proposed by Kamiran and Calders, that rebalances a training set so that a protected group and everyone else have the same rate of positive outcomes, such as being hired or approved. A ranking model first scores every example by how likely it is to have a positive label. The method then compares the size of each group-and-outcome combination with the size it would have if group and outcome were unrelated. It adds copies of positive examples from the disadvantaged group and negative examples from the favoured group, and removes negative examples from the disadvantaged group and positive examples from the favoured group, always starting with those closest to the decision boundary. Labels are never changed, so a standard classifier can learn from the rebalanced set.

example_use_cases.description: A graduate recruiter's historical shortlisting data shows women were shortlisted less often than men with similar scores. The team trains a ranking model, then copies the shortlisted women and rejected men closest to the decision boundary and removes the rejected women and shortlisted men closest to it, until the shortlisting rates match. No label is changed, and the production model is trained on the resampled set.

A bank training a loan-approval model on ten years of decisions finds that applicants under 25 were approved far less often than older applicants. Compliance wants the recorded decisions left untouched, so the model team resamples the training set until approval rates match across age groups and keeps the original labels as the record of what was decided.

limitations.description: Duplicating examples invites overfitting, and removing them discards information. The method copies the same borderline examples and drops others, so a model may memorise duplicates or lose cases it needed, which matters most when the training set is small or many changes are needed.

It assumes the whole gap in positive rates between groups is discrimination. It resamples until outcome and group are unrelated, even where part of the gap has a legitimate explanation such as differing experience, and the original authors note that this constraint is often too strong.

The result depends on a ranking model learned from the same biased data. The ranker decides which examples count as borderline, so a weak or biased ranker copies and removes the wrong ones, and in the original experiments the method worked best with unstable learners such as decision trees.

It handles one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome. Gender and ethnicity together are not covered, so resampling for one attribute can leave intersectional groups unbalanced, and the authors call multiple combined attributes a harder open problem.

Fairness is achieved on the training data, not guaranteed on new data. In the original Census Income experiment with decision trees, discrimination fell from about 16 to about 3 per cent, not to zero, and the protected attribute must be recorded for every training example.

resources.abstract:

from y and on this basis decides if this subgroup with certain class (+ or -) should be more or less numerous. Than performs oversampling or undersampling depending on the case.

sample_claims.text: In the resampled training set the rate of positive outcomes is the same for women and men, and no recorded label was changed.
The resampled loan-decision training set shows no gap in approval rates between applicants under and over 25, measured on the training data before any model was fitted.
Only a small share of the training examples were duplicated or removed, and each was chosen because it lay close to the ranking model's decision boundary.

techniques.name: Attribute Removal (Fairness Through Unawareness)
techniques.description: Attribute removal, also called fairness through unawareness, trains and runs a model without the protected attributes, such as race, gender or age, among its inputs. This meets the unawareness criterion, under which an algorithm counts as fair so long as it does not explicitly use a protected attribute, and it rules out direct discrimination on those attributes. It does not make outcomes fair. Other features can act as proxies, meaning they correlate with a removed attribute and let the model reconstruct it, for example a postcode standing in for ethnicity. For that reason the technique is best seen as the simplest baseline, to be combined with methods that look at outcomes.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment agency's data team builds a CV-ranking model for graduate roles and leaves gender, ethnicity and age out of its inputs, so that shortlisting cannot use them directly. It records that education institution and postcode may still carry some of that information and treats this as an open risk, to be handled with other methods.

A bank's credit-risk team removes sex and ethnicity from the inputs to a loan-approval model so that its decisions cannot use them directly, as its lending policy requires. It keeps the two fields in a separate monitoring table, so approval rates can still be compared across groups after launch.

A health-system analytics team builds a postpartum depression risk model from insurance claims and first tries leaving race out of the inputs. It then measures disparate impact between Black and White patients and compares the result with other bias-reduction methods on the same data, to decide whether removal is enough.

limitations.description: Proxy features keep the removed attribute's influence in the model. Postcode, school or employment history can predict race, sex or age closely enough for the model to reproduce group differences without seeing the attribute. In a published comparison on Medicaid postpartum depression data, removing race left disparate impact at about 0.6 (1 is parity), less effective than the other methods compared.

Proxies cannot be found by inspecting the feature list, because group membership can be spread across many features, and checking outcomes by group needs the very attributes that were removed. A team that deletes the column outright loses the ability to see whether the problem remains.

Removal alone is weak compliance evidence. Regulators that test for disparate impact or indirect discrimination look at outcomes, not inputs, so a model that never saw the attribute can still fail the test.

Removal can hurt the group it is meant to protect. Where the link between features and outcomes differs by group, dropping the attribute can raise error for the group concerned. Kusner et al. give a case where an 'unaware' predictor perpetuates unfairness, and Dwork et al. note that errors can come from ignoring group membership.

resources.title: Fairness Through Awareness
resources.abstract: We study fairness in classification, where individuals are classified, e.g., admitted to a university, and the goal is to prevent discrimination against individuals based on their membership in some group, while maintaining utility for the classifier (the university). The main conceptual contribution of this paper is a framework for fair classification comprising (1) a (hypothetical) task-specific metric for determining the degree to which individuals are similar with respect to the classification task at hand; (2) an algorithm for maximizing utility subject to the fairness constraint, that similar individuals are treated similarly. We also present an adaptation of our approach to achieve the complementary goal of "fair affirmative action," which guarantees statistical parity (i.e., the demographics of the set of individuals receiving any classification are the same as the demographics of the underlying population), while treating similar individuals as similarly as possible. Finally, we discuss the relationship of fairness to privacy: when fairness implies privacy, and how tools developed in the context of differential privacy may be applied to fairness.

resources.title: Counterfactual Fairness
resources.abstract: Machine learning can impact people with legal or ethical consequences when it is used to automate decisions in areas such as insurance, lending, hiring, and predictive policing. In many of these scenarios, previous decisions have been made that are unfairly biased against certain subpopulations, for example those of a particular race, gender, or sexual orientation. Since this past data may be biased, machine learning predictors must account for this to avoid perpetuating or creating discriminatory practices. In this paper, we develop a framework for modeling fairness using tools from causal inference. Our definition of counterfactual fairness captures the intuition that a decision is fair towards an individual if it the same in (a) the actual world and (b) a counterfactual world where the individual belonged to a different demographic group. We demonstrate our framework on a real-world problem of fair prediction of success in law school.

resources.title: Comparison of Methods to Reduce Bias From Clinical Prediction Models of Postpartum Depression
resources.abstract: Importance: The lack of standards in methods to reduce bias for clinical algorithms presents various challenges in providing reliable predictions and in addressing health disparities. Objective: To evaluate approaches for reducing bias in machine learning models using a real-world clinical scenario. Design, Setting, and Participants: Health data for this cohort study were obtained from the IBM MarketScan Medicaid Database. Eligibility criteria were as follows: (1) Female individuals aged 12 to 55 years with a live birth record identified by delivery-related codes from January 1, 2014, through December 31, 2018; (2) greater than 80% enrollment through pregnancy to 60 days post partum; and (3) evidence of coverage for depression screening and mental health services. Statistical analysis was performed in 2020. Exposures: Binarized race (Black individuals and White individuals). Main Outcomes and Measures: Machine learning models (logistic regression [LR], random forest, and extreme gradient boosting) were trained for 2 binary outcomes: postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum mental health service utilization. Risk-adjusted generalized linear models were used for each outcome to assess potential disparity in the cohort associated with binarized race (Black or White). Methods for reducing bias, including reweighing, Prejudice Remover, and removing race from the models, were examined by analyzing changes in fairness metrics compared with the base models. Baseline characteristics of female individuals at the top-predicted risk decile were compared for systematic differences. Fairness metrics of disparate impact (DI, 1 indicates fairness) and equal opportunity difference (EOD, 0 indicates fairness). Results: Among 573 634 female individuals initially examined for this study, 314 903 were White (54.9%), 217 899 were Black (38.0%), and the mean (SD) age was 26.1 (5.5) years. The risk-adjusted odds ratio comparing White participants with Black participants was 2.06 (95% CI, 2.02-2.10) for clinically recognized PPD and 1.37 (95% CI, 1.33-1.40) for postpartum mental health service utilization. Taking the LR model for PPD prediction as an example, reweighing reduced bias as measured by improved DI and EOD metrics from 0.31 and -0.19 to 0.79 and 0.02, respectively. Removing race from the models had inferior performance for reducing bias compared with the other methods (PPD: DI = 0.61; EOD = -0.05; mental health service utilization: DI = 0.63; EOD = -0.04). Conclusions and Relevance: Clinical prediction models trained on potentially biased data may produce unfair outcomes on the basis of the chosen metrics. This study's results suggest that the performance varied depending on the model, outcome label, and method for reducing bias. This approach toward evaluating algorithmic bias can be used as an example for the growing number of researchers who wish to examine and address bias in their data and models.

sample_claims.text: The model makes decisions without direct access to protected demographic attributes such as race, gender, or age
The lending system excludes ethnicity and gender information from all decision-making processes to prevent explicit discrimination in credit approvals
The diagnostic risk model takes no race or ethnicity field as input, as confirmed from its documented feature list, and any remaining group differences in its outputs are assessed separately.
The eligibility-scoring model used by the benefits agency has no input field for age, sex or ethnicity, as confirmed from its documented feature list.

techniques.name: Fair Adversarial Networks
techniques.description: Fair Adversarial Networks is a pre-processing method, proposed by Cevora (2020), that rewrites a dataset so that a protected characteristic such as race, sex or age is hard to predict from it, including through proxies such as postcode or occupation. It trains two neural networks against each other. An autoencoder (a network that learns to reproduce its input) rewrites each record while staying as close to the original as it can, and an adversary network tries to predict the protected characteristic from the rewritten records. The autoencoder is penalised both for changing the data and for the adversary's success, so over alternating rounds of training it strips out the information the adversary relies on and changes little else. The output is the rewritten dataset, which any downstream analysis or model can use unchanged, and in the paper success means a freshly trained adversary does no better than always guessing the most common category.

example_use_cases.description: A probation service's analytics team wants to model reoffending from defendant records in which race is encoded indirectly, through charge descriptions and neighbourhood. It runs the records through a Fair Adversarial Network before modelling and confirms that a freshly trained classifier predicts race from the transformed data no better than always guessing the most common group.

An HR analytics team at a courier company building an absenteeism model removes information about employees' age group from its personnel records, including through proxies such as length of service and family circumstances, so that the standard modelling tools its analysts already use can run on the transformed data unchanged.

A local education authority allocating support funding with a model of school performance data de-biases the data with respect to each school's majority ethnic composition before modelling, and keeps the adversary's chance-level result and the reconstruction error with the funding model's documentation as evidence of what was removed and how much the data changed.

limitations.description: No public implementation is known. The paper withholds the parts that make training practical (an approximation of how well a fully trained adversary would do, a stabilising mechanism and regularisers) as its company's intellectual property, saying only that standard approaches can replicate the result on a one-off basis with heavy tuning, and the company's web tool is no longer online. Adopting the method means reimplementing it from the paper.

It removes every detectable relationship with the protected characteristic, including relationships that are legitimate or deliberately protective; the author notes it also removes positive discrimination. Where the characteristic carries legitimate information, such as sex in some clinical data, that information goes along with the bias, and the accuracy drops seen on the demonstration datasets cannot be split into bias removed and signal lost.

Success is judged against one adversary: in the paper, a single-hidden-layer network trained from three random starts. A more capable model may still recover the characteristic, and the author states that residual discrimination is likely still present, so a chance-level adversary is weaker evidence than it appears. The paper reports no downstream accuracy or fairness results; the only application evidence is the same company's Rosa demonstration.

Every variable in every record can be altered by the autoencoder, so the de-biased dataset no longer contains the original values. Individual records cannot be checked against source data, feature meanings drift, and any explanation of a downstream model refers to transformed features rather than to the applicant's actual postcode or income.

Adversarial training is unstable and its settings have no principled choice: the weight balancing reconstruction against the adversary, the network architectures and the stopping point all need tuning per dataset. The paper keeps the lowest-loss state to guard against run-away training and describes its own convergence as fairly sub-optimal.

resources.title: Fair Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: The influence of human judgement is ubiquitous in datasets used across the analytics industry, yet humans are known to be sub-optimal decision makers prone to various biases. Analysing biased datasets then leads to biased outcomes of the analysis. Bias by protected characteristics (e.g. race) is of particular interest as it may not only make the output of analytical process sub-optimal, but also illegal. Countering the bias by constraining the analytical outcomes to be fair is problematic because A) fairness lacks a universally accepted definition, while at the same time some definitions are mutually exclusive, and B) the use of optimisation constraints ensuring fairness is incompatible with most analytical pipelines. Both problems are solved by methods which remove bias from the data and returning an altered dataset. This approach aims to not only remove the actual bias variable (e.g. race), but also alter all proxy variables (e.g. postcode) so the bias variable is not detectable from the rest of the data. The advantage of using this approach is that the definition of fairness as a lack of detectable bias in the data (as opposed to the output of analysis) is universal and therefore solves problem (A). Furthermore, as the data is altered to remove bias the problem (B) disappears because the analytical pipelines can remain unchanged. This approach has been adopted by several technical solutions. None of them, however, seems to be satisfactory in terms of ability to remove multivariate, non-linear and non-binary biases. Therefore, in this paper I propose the concept of Fair Adversarial Networks as an easy-to-implement general method for removing bias from data. This paper demonstrates that Fair Adversarial Networks achieve this aim.

resources.title: Demonstrating Rosa: the fairness solution for any Data Analytic pipeline
resources.abstract: Most datasets of interest to the analytics industry are impacted by various forms of human bias. The outcomes of Data Analytics [DA] or Machine Learning [ML] on such data are therefore prone to replicating the bias. As a result, a large number of biased decision-making systems based on DA/ML have recently attracted attention. In this paper we introduce Rosa, a free, web-based tool to easily de-bias datasets with respect to a chosen characteristic. Rosa is based on the principles of Fair Adversarial Networks, developed by illumr Ltd., and can therefore remove interactive, non-linear, and non-binary bias. Rosa is stand-alone pre-processing step / API, meaning it can be used easily with any DA/ML pipeline. We test the efficacy of Rosa in removing bias from data-driven decision making systems by performing standard DA tasks on five real-world datasets, selected for their relevance to current DA problems, and also their high potential for bias. We use simple ML models to model a characteristic of analytical interest, and compare the level of bias in the model output both with and without Rosa as a pre-processing step. We find that in all cases there is a substantial decrease in bias of the data-driven decision making systems when the data is pre-processed with Rosa.

sample_claims.text: A classifier trained on the de-biased reoffending dataset cannot predict defendants' race better than always guessing the majority group.

The personnel records used to train the absenteeism model were rewritten so that a freshly trained classifier predicts employees' age group, including through proxies such as length of service, no better than always guessing the most common group.

The school funding data stayed close to the original after de-biasing, with the reconstruction error recorded and judged acceptable by the analysts, while the adversary's accuracy at predicting majority ethnic composition fell to chance.
